prompt.context: Your client is a private company that manufactures switches for machine tools. The switches serve one purpose: to stop the machine instantly. Failure to do so may result in damage to the machine and/or the machine operator.
prompt.question:
Given the following constraints, how can the company make more money?
• No changes can be made to the product line
• You only have your current customers
• No international expansion

clarifying_info.q: Have our switches or our competitors' switches ever failed?
clarifying_info.a: No, our switches (and our competitors' switches) have never failed.

clarifying_info.q: Do customers buy exclusively from us?
clarifying_info.a: Our customers have dealt exclusively with us for several years, although there is no exclusivity contract.

clarifying_info.q: How strong is the relationship between our sales force and customers?
clarifying_info.a: The sales force has strong relationships with the customers, so they just take the orders each year.

clarifying_info.q: What is the cost of the machine tools our customers make?
clarifying_info.a: Cost of machine tools that our customer makes: $60,000.

clarifying_info.q: What is the competitive pricing and market share landscape?
clarifying_info.a: Company: Our Company, Price/switch: $100, Market Share: 30% ($1B market). Competitor 1: $120, 60%. Competitor 2: $80, 10%.

framework: Revenue = Price x Quantity; explore levers on both sides given the constraints
Quantity lever: can existing customers expand their purchases? (exclusivity capture, untapped machines at existing sites)
Price lever: assess price sensitivity by analyzing competitor pricing vs. market share; higher-priced competitor holds largest share suggesting low price sensitivity
Acquisition lever: acquiring a competitor could consolidate market share and enable pricing power
Sanity check: validate with value-based pricing — switch cost vs. machine tool cost ($60k) implies large willingness to pay

questions.prompt: What are the possible ways to increase quantity sold, given you cannot add new customers or expand internationally?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify two sub-levers: (1) capture a greater share of existing customers' demand if customers split purchases across competitors — potentially via an exclusivity arrangement; (2) identify untapped machines at existing customer sites that could use the switch but don't yet.

questions.prompt: Given the competitive data, what price increase would you recommend and why?
questions.guidance: Candidate should observe that Competitor 1 charges $120 and holds 60% market share despite being the most expensive, suggesting customers are NOT price-sensitive. This indicates the client is underpriced relative to perceived quality parity. A recommended increase to ~$120-$125 is well-supported. Candidate should also note price as a quality signal and defend the upper bound relative to Competitor 1.

math.setup: Current revenue: 30% of $1B = $300M. If price increases from $100 to $125 (25% increase) with quantity unchanged: new revenue = $300M × 1.25
steps: Assuming no volume loss: new revenue = $300M × 1.25 = $375M
math.answer: Incremental revenue of ~$75M at a 25% price increase to $125, assuming no volume loss.

questions.prompt: If you could acquire one competitor, which would you choose and why?
questions.guidance: Candidate should flag antitrust risk for acquiring Competitor 1 (60% share + 30% = 90% of a $1B market). Competitor 2 is the better acquisition target. Post-acquisition, the combined entity (our 30% + C2's 10% = 40%) could raise price of C2 switches to align with the new company price (~$125), while remaining slightly below Competitor 1 ($120 after our increase). Risks include alienating C2's price-sensitive customers.

math.setup: Post-acquisition combined market share = 30% + 10% = 40% of $1B = $400M revenue base. Raise combined price to $125.
steps: Raise C2 price to $125: revenue from C2 segment = $100M × (125/80) = $156M (if volume held)
math.answer: Acquiring Competitor 2 and raising combined price to ~$125 yields an estimated ~$131M revenue uplift over the current combined baseline, while staying price-competitive with Competitor 1 at $120.

brainstorming.prompt: What factors might explain why Competitor 1 commands both the highest price and the largest market share, and what should we verify before recommending a price increase?

categories.name: Sales & distribution
ideas: Larger or more effective sales force

categories.name: Brand & market position
ideas: Entrenched as industry standard or preferred supplier
Perceived as quality leader despite comparable actual performance
Price seen as proxy for reliability in a safety-critical product

categories.name: Service & support
ideas: Superior after-sales service or warranty terms

categories.name: Customer segmentation
ideas: Competitor 1 may serve less price-sensitive segments (e.g., larger manufacturers)
Our 30% share may skew toward more price-sensitive buyers
Different end-market verticals with different willingness to pay

recommendation: Raise the switch price by 20–25% (from $100 to ~$120–$125) immediately, bringing it in line with Competitor 1's pricing; given comparable quality and strong customer relationships, volume loss risk is low
If an acquisition is pursued, target Competitor 2 (antitrust risk rules out Competitor 1); integrate and align pricing to ~$125 to capture the full 40% share at a premium price point
risks: Some existing customers may test alternatives if price increases are perceived as opportunistic, though the lack of an exclusivity contract increases this risk
Acquiring Competitor 2 and raising its prices could alienate C2's current customer base, who chose C2 partly on price
Competitor 1 could respond to a narrowing price gap by cutting prices or increasing service levels
next_steps: Conduct customer interviews or surveys to quantify price elasticity before implementing the increase
Analyze Competitor 1's operational differences (sales force size, service model) to determine if any capability gaps need closing
Model acquisition economics for Competitor 2 including synergies, integration costs, and customer retention assumptions
